The building is not equipped with a centralized heating and cooling system. Heating and cooling within individual suites are provided by in-suite Magic-Pak units, which consist of a gas-fired furnace for space heating and an integral DX cooling section for space cooling, operating independently in each suite.

While this decentralized configuration provides basic temperature control, gas-fired furnace and conventional DX cooling systems are generally less efficient than heat pump–based solutions. Typical non-condensing gas furnaces operate at thermal efficiencies in the range of 78–82%, while standard DX cooling sections often achieve cooling COP values of approximately 2.8–3.5, depending on equipment age and condition. In comparison, modern high-efficiency air-source heat pump (ASHP) systems can achieve heating and cooling COP values exceeding 4.0–5.0 under favorable conditions.

In addition to moderate energy performance, the distributed nature of Magic-Pak units increases overall maintenance and lifecycle costs, as each suite contains its own combustion appliance, heat exchanger, blower motor, and refrigeration components. Annual servicing, combustion inspections, heat exchanger monitoring, and potential component replacement contribute to higher long-term operating expenses compared to centralized or heat pump–based systems.

Given the age and inherent efficiency limitations of gas-fired packaged units, replacement with a modern heat pump–based system should be considered in the short term as part of a mechanical system modernization strategy to improve energy efficiency, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and lower long-term maintenance and operating costs.

measures.existing_conditions: The existing HVAC mechanical systems—including MUAs, exhaust fans, heating boilers, DHW plant, cooling equipment, and pumps—are controlled manually or via basic local thermostats and temperature sensors. There is minimal outdoor-air reset, limited boiler sequencing, and no centralized scheduling or monitoring. Equipment often operates during unoccupied periods, leading to excessive energy use and chronic overheating.
measures.notes: Install a new central BAS to Control boilers, DHW, MUAs, pumps and exhaust fans with scheduling, reset and remote access, reducing energy use and maintenance. Improve building operation and management.
measures.retrofit_conditions:

The BAS would provide occupancy-based scheduling, outdoor-temperature reset for boilers, zone-level temperature modulation, real-time monitoring, remote access, and alarm notifications. Improved control will reduce unnecessary run time, lower energy consumption, and improve comfort while reducing maintenance costs through better diagnostics. measures.existing_conditions:
The domestic hot water (DHW) system is served by an indirect storage tank connected to the central boiler plant. The storage tank, associated DHW circulation pumps, and portions of the DHW piping were observed to be original to the building and approaching the end of their expected service life. 
In addition, two (2) atmospheric LAARS gas-fired DHW boilers, installed in 2003 with an estimated thermal efficiency of approximately 78%, are approaching the end of their expected service life. As atmospheric boilers, these units operate without condensing capability and therefore at lower thermal efficiency compared to modern condensing DHW boiler systems.
Aging indirect storage tanks typically require periodic internal relining and increased maintenance effort to maintain performance and water quality. As these components continue to age, maintenance requirements, the risk of unplanned service interruptions, and lifecycle costs are expected to increase.
measures.measure_title: Replace aging storage tank, install new plate & frame Heat exchanger and Condensing DHW boiler retrofit
measures.notes: Replace aging indirect DHW storage tanks and atmospheric DHW boilers with glass-lined storage tanks, a plate-and-frame heat exchanger, and high-efficiency condensing DHW boilers to improve temperature stability, reduce maintenance requirements, and increase DHW system efficiency to approximately 98%.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
As part of the boiler plant and hydronic system reconfiguration, Mann recommends upgrading the DHW system through a comprehensive DHW modernization approach, including:
•	Replacement of the existing aging indirect storage tank with vertical glass-lined DHW storage tanks served by a plate-and-frame heat exchanger; 
•	Replacement of the existing atmospheric DHW boilers with high-efficiency condensing DHW boilers, capable of achieving thermal efficiencies of up to approximately 98% under suitable operating conditions.
Under the proposed configuration, the condensing DHW boilers would generate hot water for transfer through the plate-and-frame heat exchanger, which would efficiently heat domestic water stored in the glass-lined vertical storage tanks. This arrangement provides improved heat-transfer performance, more stable DHW temperature control, and greater operational flexibility compared to aging indirect tank designs.
Upgrading to condensing DHW boilers allows the system to operate effectively at lower return-water temperatures, enabling latent heat recovery and significantly improving overall system efficiency. Together, these upgrades reduce long-term maintenance requirements, improve system reliability, lower natural gas consumption, and align with the overall mechanical room modernization strategy by supporting a more modular, efficient, and serviceable DHW system layout.

measures.measure_title: Convert In-Suite MagicPak Units to Air-Source Heat Pump (ASHP) Systems
measures.notes: Replace in-suite Magic-Pak gas-fired furnace/DX units with high-efficiency air-source heat pump systems to improve energy performance, reduce maintenance costs, and support long-term building electrification.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends replacing the existing Magic-Pak units with modern air-source heat pump (ASHP) systems. ASHP systems provide both heating and cooling through a high-efficiency refrigeration cycle and eliminate the need for in-suite gas combustion.

Modern cold-climate ASHP systems can achieve heating and cooling COP values exceeding 4.0–5.0 under favorable conditions, significantly improving energy efficiency compared to existing gas-fired furnace and DX configurations. In addition, eliminating gas combustion reduces greenhouse gas emissions and simplifies mechanical maintenance.

The proposed retrofit would improve suite-level temperature control, reduce long-term maintenance costs, and align the building with electrification and decarbonization strategies. Phased implementation may be considered to align with reserve fund planning and suite turnover cycles.

measures.existing_conditions:
The building is served by a  Air handling unit (AHU) that provides ventilation air to corridors and other common areas. The AHU is equipped with gas burner, condenser units and variable frequency drive (VFD)–controlled supply fans, and operates with local, stand-alone controls.

While VFD control is present at the fan level, the existing AHU relies on conventional heating and cooling operation. In addition, the AHU is not integrated into a centralized Building Automation System (BAS), which limits opportunities for optimized scheduling, supply air temperature reset, demand-based ventilation, and coordinated system operation.
measures.measure_title: Current AHU has VFD, upgrade to Hybrid MUA and with BAS Integration
measures.notes: Retrofit the existing AHU to a heat pump–based system with BAS integration to improve heating efficiency, ventilation control, and long-term operational flexibility.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends retrofitting the existing AHU to operate as a heat pump–based hydronic AHU system. with condensing gas burner as back up. Under the proposed configuration, the MUA heating coil would be served by a dedicated hydronic heat pump, allowing the unit to deliver heating efficiently at lower supply water temperatures while retaining the existing MUA casing, hydronic coil, and VFD-controlled supply fan, subject to detailed engineering review.

The existing VFD-controlled supply fan would be retained, and the MUA would be integrated into a Building Automation System (BAS) to enable coordinated scheduling, discharge air temperature reset, demand-based ventilation control, and alarm monitoring. This retrofit would improve overall energy efficiency, enhance ventilation control, and support future low-temperature heating strategies.

This approach minimizes equipment replacement, reduces disruption to building operations, and provides a cost-effective pathway to improve MUA performance, controllability, and long-term operational flexibility.

https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

Further engineering review is required to confirm system configuration, heat pump sizing, control strategy, and electrical capacity requirements.

measures.existing_conditions: Common area lighting (e.g., corridors, stairwells, storage rooms, parking areas, and ancillary spaces) is primarily controlled through manual switches or time-based schedules, resulting in lighting operating during unoccupied periods. Limited occupancy-based control leads to unnecessary electrical energy use and increased lamp operating hours.
measures.notes: Install occupancy-based motion sensors for common area lighting to reduce unnecessary runtime, lower electrical consumption, and extend lighting equipment life.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends installing occupancy / motion sensors to control common area lighting where appropriate. The motion sensors would automatically turn lighting on when spaces are occupied and off or dim when spaces are unoccupied, reducing unnecessary runtime while maintaining occupant safety and visibility.

This measure would reduce electrical energy consumption, extend lamp and ballast/driver life, and lower ongoing maintenance requirements. Motion control is particularly effective in intermittently occupied spaces such as stairwells, corridors, storage rooms, and parking areas.

Where applicable, motion sensors may be integrated with existing lighting control strategies or future centralized control systems to further enhance operational flexibility.

measures.existing_conditions: Domestic cold water is currently pressurized by a constant-speed booster pump with a downstream pressure-reducing or regulating valve to maintain setpoint pressure. The valve introduces unnecessary head loss and wastes pumping energy, and the pump operates at full speed even when demand is low.
measures.notes: Convert the constant-speed domestic booster pump to VFD control, eliminating throttling losses and matching pressure to demand for significant pump-energy savings.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install a variable frequency drive (VFD) on the domestic water booster pump and remove or bypass the pressure regulating valve. The VFD will control pump speed to maintain the desired discharge pressure directly, allowing the pump to slow down during periods of low demand. This reduces energy use, pump wear and noise while maintaining adequate system pressure. Further engineering is required to confirm setpoints, sensor locations and control logic.

The windows were observed to be in generally fair condition at the time of the site visit. However, in aging buildings, the insulating glazing units (IGUs) may gradually lose performance over time due to seal deterioration and potential reduction of the insulating gas between panes. While no widespread failure was observed, long-term thermal performance may decline as glazing systems age.
measures.measure_title: Window Lifecycle Planning and Sealant Renewal (Aging Double-Glazed Units)
measures.notes: Monitor aging double-pane windows and incorporate sealant renewal and long-term glazing upgrades into lifecycle and capital planning strategies.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
As part of ongoing building envelope maintenance and long-term capital planning, it is recommended to monitor window performance and implement periodic re-caulking and weatherstripping renewal where required. Full window replacement is not considered immediately necessary; however, future glazing upgrades should be evaluated in alignment with reserve fund studies and envelope lifecycle planning. Proactive lifecycle management will help maintain thermal performance, occupant comfort, and overall energy efficiency over time.

New glazing systems with improved low-E coatings, warm-edge spacers, and enhanced seal performance would significantly reduce heat loss, improve occupant comfort, and lower heating demand. Phased implementation can be considered to align with reserve fund planning and envelope lifecycle scheduling.

This reduces energy use, pump wear and noise while maintaining adequate system pressure. Further engineering is required to confirm setpoints, sensor locations and control logic.

measures.retrofit_conditions:

ventilation_items.text:
The units are equipped with supply fans with variable frequency drives (VFDs), integral gas-fired heating burners, and Air Cooled Chiller provide cooling capacity. The VFD, gas-fired heating burner, and air cooled chiller were observed to be in fair to good condition.

Equipment appeared to be functioning as intended during the site walkthrough, with no visible signs of mechanical distress.
ventilation_items.title: VFD+Gas Fire+Air Cooled Chiller

ventilation_items.text:
Although the AHU units are in generally good mechanical condition, the building is not equipped with a centralized Building Automation System (BAS) to coordinate AHU operation with the rest of the mechanical systems.

Integration of the existing VFD-controlled AHU units into a BAS would enable improved scheduling, supply air temperature reset, demand-based ventilation, and alarm monitoring. These enhancements would improve overall energy performance, operational oversight, and long-term system reliability.
ventilation_items.title: Ventilation controls via BAS
